title: PAMod: Modeling Cyclical Shifts via Phase-Amplitude Modulation for Non-stationary Time Series Forecasting
claim: Train and test distributions differ, yet mean and variance follow stable, decoupled cyclical patterns tied to periodic position.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; histogram left, dual-axis periodic line plot right
description: Two side-by-side plots using real ETTh1 OT-channel data. Panel (a), 'Distribution Shifts', overlays histograms and smoothed density curves for the training set (blue) and test set (magenta). Dashed vertical lines mark each set's mean. The test distribution sits visibly to the left of the training one, with a different spread. Panel (b), '72-Hour Mean-Std Variation', is a dual-axis line chart. The mean is a blue line on the left axis and the std is a green line on the right axis, over three consecutive 24-hour cycles. Dotted vertical lines separate the cycles, which are labeled Cycle 1, 2 and 3. The two curves repeat nearly identically in each cycle, and mean and std move out of phase with each other. The eye goes first to the contrasting overlapping histograms, then to the repeating waves.
caption: Visualization of distribution shift and periodic mean-std variation in the OT channel of ETTh1. (a) histograms and density curves illustrate distinct probability distributions, with dashed lines marking the respective means in training and test sets. (b) 72-hour cyclic variations exhibit stable 24-hour repetition across three consecutive cycles (Cycle 1–3), highlighting inherent diurnal periodicity. Notably, distribution shifts originate from decoupled mean and variance variations within these cycles.
abstract: Real-world time series forecasting faces the fundamental challenge of non-stationary statistical properties, including shifts in mean and variance over time. While reversible instance normalization (RevIN) has shown promise by stationarizing inputs and denormalizing outputs, it relies on the strong assumption that historical and future distributions remain identical. We observe that in many practical applications, distribution shifts follow cyclical patterns that correlate with periodic positions (e.g., seasonal and holiday volatility). To this end, we propose PAMod, a lightweight yet powerful framework that models cyclical distribution shifts via Phase-Amplitude Modulation in the normalized feature space. PAMod learns periodic embeddings to modulate representations: phase modulation captures mean shifts, while amplitude modulation adapts to variance changes. Crucially, we prove mathematically that modulating in normalized space is equivalent to applying dynamic denormalization, offering an elegant unification of distribution adaptation and representation learning. Extensive experiments on twelve real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PAMod achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer computational resources. Furthermore, our modulation mechanism, as a novel plug-and-play technique, can improve existing time-series forecasting methods with simple integration.
